You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Amazon Q2 Earnings Preview: AWS Acceleration vs. AI Capex Trade-off

TEXT:
1. Investment Highlights Snapshot
Amazon will report its second-quarter results after the U.S. market close on July 30, 2026. Wall Street consensus expects revenue of approximately $196–197 billion (+17% YoY, versus $167.7 billion a year earlier) and diluted EPS of about $1.82 (+8.3% YoY, versus $1.68). The company’s prior guidance calls for net sales of $194–199 billion (+16%–19% YoY) and operating income of $20–24 billion .
The key debate is not whether headline revenue will land inside the guided range, but whether AWS can continue accelerating and whether the full-year capital expenditure target of roughly $200 billion will be raised further. Alphabet ’s recent capex hike and subsequent share-price reaction have made investors more sensitive to the combination of strong growth and elevated spending.
2. Four Key Focus Areas
Focus 1: Can AWS Growth Re-accelerate?
AWS revenue reached $37.6 billion in Q1 (+28% YoY), the fastest pace in 15 quarters. Consensus now looks for further acceleration to 31%–33% in Q2 (roughly $40–41 billion ). Some houses have already lifted their forecasts to 33%, citing sustained Anthropic and OpenAI workloads flowing through Bedrock and ongoing enterprise AI demand. A print in this range would reinforce the narrative that AI demand is converting into durable cloud revenue; a figure below 28% would raise questions about the durability of the re-acceleration.
Focus 2: AI Capital Spending and Free-Cash-Flow Pressure
Management previously guided to approximately $200 billion of capital expenditure for full-year 2026, primarily for data centers, custom silicon (Trainium and related chips), and supporting infrastructure. Several analysts now expect the figure could rise toward $210 billion on higher memory costs and stronger demand. Free cash flow already collapsed to $1.2 billion in Q1. Markets will scrutinize the actual Q2 spend and any update to the full-year outlook. Elevated spending can be tolerated if framed as growth-oriented investment backed by customer commitments (RPO stood at $364 billion at the end of Q1); a material upward revision risks an Alphabet-style sell-off.
Focus 3: Retail and Advertising Resilience
Online stores are expected to generate roughly $69.8 billion (+13% YoY), while advertising revenue is seen near $19.2–19.3 billion (around +22% YoY). Prime Day was pulled forward into Q2, providing a potential retail tailwind, though household spend data points to greater value-seeking behavior. Stability in North America and International retail operating margins will be important in determining whether overall operating income lands near the midpoint of guidance.
Focus 4: Q3 Guidance and Non-Operating Items
Beyond core operating metrics, attention will turn to the Q3 revenue and profit outlook, as well as any mark-to-market impact from the Anthropic equity stake on EPS. Q1 included a sizable non-operating gain; a similar swing in Q2 would lead investors to place greater weight on the underlying operating picture.
3. Risks and Opportunities
Upside Catalysts:
AWS growth at or above 33%, accompanied by constructive commentary on Bedrock and custom-chip progress.
Full-year capex guidance raised only modestly or held near $200 billion, with emphasis on locked-in customer commitments.
Retail margin improvement or stronger-than-expected advertising growth that lifts operating income toward the high end of the guided range.
Downside Risks:
Capex guidance lifted significantly above $210 billion, intensifying concerns over near-term free-cash-flow pressure and payback periods.
AWS growth falling short of 30% or margins coming under material pressure.
Conservative Q3 guidance or incremental regulatory/macro headwinds weighing on the retail business.
4. Trading Strategy Considerations
Bull Case: AWS growth clearly accelerates (≥32%–33%), the capex increase remains contained, and management underscores the high returns and customer lock-in associated with AI investments. In this scenario, the stock could look through the spending concerns and re-rate toward a growth premium.
Bear Case: A sizable capex upward revision combined with softer-than-expected AWS growth, or continued free-cash-flow pressure, would likely prompt the market to prioritize the “high spend, delayed monetization” narrative and produce a short-term pullback.
Key Metrics to Watch:
AWS revenue and year-over-year growth rate
Operating income relative to the $20–24 billion guidance range
Any update to full-year capex guidance
Q3 revenue and profit outlook, plus changes in RPO
Positioning Notes: Options markets are pricing roughly a 6%–7% move around the print. Short-term traders should focus on the post-market and next-day reaction, particularly the AWS-plus-capex combination. Medium-term investors should prioritize management commentary on the return time line for AI investments rather than reacting solely to headline revenue or EPS. Position sizing and risk controls remain essential.
